item.title: Early tetrapod neck mobility modelled using an extant analogue
item.dc:creator: Dana E. Korneisel
Cassandra M. Donatelli
Linfang Han
Thomas A. Stewart
Andrew L. Traynor
Benjamin K. A. Otoo
Marcos Martinez
Tetsuto Miyashita
item.description:
Authors: Dana E. Korneisel, Cassandra M. Donatelli, Linfang Han, Thomas A. Stewart, Andrew L. Traynor, Benjamin K. A. Otoo, Marcos Martinez, Tetsuto Miyashita, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Tetrapods arose from lobe-finned fishes with a notochord-dominated axial column 1–3 . During this transition, the skull became separated from the shoulder girdle 4–6 , giving rise to a neck region. This head–shoulder separation has generated hypotheses suggesting that neck mobility increased during the origin of tetrapods, facilitating the ecological transition towards more terrestrial habitats 4,5,7–9 . However, incompletely co-ossified vertebral components 10 have posed a challenge to modelling the mobility of these early tetrapod necks. Here we used material tests on the similarly configured axial columns of sturgeon to predict the capacities of the tetrapod neck region for lateral flexion, extension and rotation across the tetrapod stem. Our model indicates that the soft tissue-dominated axial column was surprisingly rigid, despite lacking co-ossified vertebral components. We estimate that most stem tetrapods could move their heads less than 6° laterally and less than 3° dorsally but could not rotate them. Notably, mobility did not shift in conjunction with the head–shoulder separation that occurred between the origin of tristichopterids (represented by Eusthenopteron ) and that of more crownward stem tetrapods. Therefore, mobility in the tetrapod neck did not serve as a functional driver of head–shoulder separation. Instead, forelimb-driven locomotion, implicated in early tetrapods 11–14 , provides a better functional explanation for the head–shoulder separation.

item.title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
item.dc:creator: David H. Cook
Xiaoyu Chen
Michael O’Leary
Satish Rao
Wenqing Wang
Calvin H. Belcher
Madelyn Payne
Pedro Borges
item.description:
Authors: David H. Cook, Xiaoyu Chen, Michael O’Leary, Satish Rao, Wenqing Wang, Calvin H. Belcher, Madelyn Payne, Pedro Borges, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Plastic deformation in body-centred cubic (bcc) metals and alloys is conventionally mediated by screw dislocations. Their temperature-sensitive motion is attributed to a steep rise in strength with decreasing temperature that constricts plastic zones at crack tips, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition 1 . Here we evaluated the mechanical properties of group IV–V bcc refractory alloys with similar electronic structures at 20 K and found that these materials instead exhibit a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition. This behaviour arises from the global activation of twinning and an ω-phase transformation, which nucleate dislocations at interfaces before global dislocation motion. The initial mechanism is temperature insensitive and controls yielding, thereby preventing a crack-tip plastic zone from constricting with decreasing temperature.

item.title: Engineered TYK2 dependence enables myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonism
item.dc:creator: D. Alejandro Canaria
Trang T. T. Nguyen
Huang Huang
Hui Xu
Lili Yue
Yongyao Fu
Hoa Truong
Kerul Patel
item.description:
Authors: D. Alejandro Canaria, Trang T. T. Nguyen, Huang Huang, Hui Xu, Lili Yue, Yongyao Fu, Hoa Truong, Kerul Patel, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Interleukin-10 (IL-10) is a central anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses immune responses in myeloid cells but can also activate T cells, limiting its therapeutic use in chronic inflammatory diseases owing to narrow efficacy windows and dose-limiting toxicities 1–5 . Here we show that myeloid and T cells differ in their dependence on JAK-family kinase pairing for IL-10 signalling and function. We took advantage of this differential kinase dependence to engineer a tetravalent nanobody-based myeloid-selective IL-10 receptor agonist (msIL-10R agonist) that fully recapitulates IL-10’s potent suppression of monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells while avoiding stimulation of T cells. Cryo-electron microscopy structural analysis reveals a distinct receptor cross-linking geometry of the msIL-10R agonist compared with native IL-10 family cytokines. This tetravalent architecture renders signalling strictly TYK2-dependent and highly sensitive to IL-10Rα and IL-10Rβ receptor abundance, thereby conferring selective activity in myeloid cells. This msIL-10R agonist reduces inflammation in humanized mouse models of lipopolysaccharide challenge, delayed-type hypersensitivity and colitis. A humanized version exhibits IgG-like pharmacokinetics, sustained receptor occupancy and durable myeloid suppression up to 30 days without T cell activation or haematological toxicities in non-human primates. These findings establish a geometry-based strategy for achieving cell-type-selective cytokine signalling and identify the msIL-10R agonist as a therapeutic candidate for myeloid-driven inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases.

item.title: Sexual dimorphism in epidermal stem cell dynamics
item.dc:creator: Dan Engelman
Joel Hochstetter
Anaïs Bauduin
Sagar Patil
Marta Valenti
Yura Song
Qiuyu Lian
Annagiada Toniolo
item.description:
Authors: Dan Engelman, Joel Hochstetter, Anaïs Bauduin, Sagar Patil, Marta Valenti, Yura Song, Qiuyu Lian, Annagiada Toniolo, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The epidermis is a stratified epithelium comprising proliferative basal cells and differentiated suprabasal cells that are continuously renewed throughout life. Conflicting theories have been proposed regarding the heterogeneity of the basal cell layer, with some studies proposing that all proliferative cells have self-renewal potential during homeostasis 1–5 . Meanwhile, others posit a model in which stem cell differentiation occurs through an intermediate transit-amplifying-like progenitor state with strictly limited proliferative potential 6–10 . Here, to determine the heterogeneity and pattern of cell fate, we performed intravital time-lapse imaging to track the fate of lineage-labelled cells in the skin interfollicular epidermis. Results from quantitative analyses of clonal dynamics support a two-compartment model of epidermal homeostasis, whereby basal cells are organized in a stem cell–transit-amplifying cell hierarchy. Critical to these conclusions was the discovery of sexual dimorphism in epidermal fate, with female mice showing a highly synchronized pattern of cell division, differentiation and delamination that contributes to accelerated wound healing. Single-cell RNA sequencing, transcriptional profiling and clonal analyses of castrated mice revealed that male sex hormones promote stem cell differentiation and delamination. In summary, our study provides insight into the functional identity of the stem cell population and identifies sex-specific differences in the regulation of epidermal stem cells and transit-amplifying cell fate.

item.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
item.dc:creator: Guillermo E. Parada
Hannes Bretschneider
Jack Daiyang Li
Jacob L. Fine
Steven J. Dupas
Jonathan D. Ellis
Ulrich Braunschweig
Sophie Bonnal
item.description:
Authors: Guillermo E. Parada, Hannes Bretschneider, Jack Daiyang Li, Jacob L. Fine, Steven J. Dupas, Jonathan D. Ellis, Ulrich Braunschweig, Sophie Bonnal, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology 1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes 1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.
